newsitem.title: FRANCE: Defence industries "hot" subject for new minister.
newsitem.headline: Defence industries "hot" subject for new minister.

text.p: France's new defence minister, moving into office on Thursday, indicated that the future of the country's arms industries was among the first subjects he would tackle.

"What about Thomson-CSF and the Rafale (combat aircraft)? Are they the 'hot' subjects you will handle immediately?" reporters asked Alain Richard after a handover ceremony with outgoing minister Charles Millon.
"Clearly I can't hide anything from you," said Richard, while adding that he would make no further comment on the subject until he had orders to do so from Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin.
The Socialist party said before its upset election victory on Sunday that it favoured continued public control over the arms industries.

The outgoing centre-right government had planned to sell its 58 percent stake in Thomson-CSF, a leading defence electronics firm, and to force Dassault Aviation to merge with state-owned plane and missile company Aerospatiale which was to be privatised.
Richard, a Socialist budget expert little known outside parliamentary circles, was a surprise appointee for the defence portfolio since he has no apparent defence experience.
French media speculated he was chosen precisely to handle such touchy issues as the future of the defence industries and defence budgets in general.
"Without flattering myself, I think Lionel Jospin believed I could face up to the challenge," Richard told reporters.
Asked his position on the possibility of France returning to NATO's military wing, Richard replied: "Don't make any final judgments on anything until you've seen the whole file."
Jospin said last month he would oppose Gaullist President Jacques Chirac's moves to return France to NATO's integrated command if he came to power.
Chirac has said Paris will make a full return if the United States hands the alliance's Naples-based Southern Command, which controls the Mediterranean, to a European officer.
Washington has so far rejected the French bid and Jospin said if the situation was frozen with Paris remaining outside full military integration, "that would suit me fully".
Under the constitution, Chirac commands the armed forces but Jospin is in charge of defence policy.

Richard indicated that, as expected, the Socialists would shoot down a proposal by Millon, now before parliament, to create five-day "Citizens' Meetings" to register youths for possible military service and lecture them on patriotism.
The registration period was a Millon brainchild following Chirac's decision to abolish conscription and move to an all-professional army by 2002.

The Socialists saw the scheme as a waste of money and Richard said the issue would be brought as soon as possible before the new left-wing dominated parliament, "which will follow the position of the new majority".

He confirmed that, unlike his predecessor, he had done his compulsory army service. Asked whether he had fond memories of it, he smiled and said: "That question is covered by the statute of limitations."
